screens.title: Project 1: Building the Elementary Logic Gates
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter guides you through Project 1: creating a complete set of elementary logic gates using only the Nand gate and the chips you build along the way. You will produce 1-bit gates like Not, And, Or, Xor, Mux, and DMux, expand those designs into 16-bit versions, and assemble multi-way selectors and demultiplexers. The emphasis is on modular, hierarchical design: each chip is tested and verified before it becomes a building block for larger chips. Practically, this means translating truth tables into Boolean expressions, turning those into HDL, and using the Hardware Simulator with test scripts to confirm behavior. As you work, keep a concise log of design choices and debugging steps. This project is foundational: the chips you complete here function as the standard library for all later hardware in the course. By learning to reduce complexity to a single primitive and then composing verified components, you sharpen both engineering discipline and conceptual clarity. Reflect as you build: what does a computer become when you trace every operation back to one simple gate?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of Project 1 you will have built a verified standard library of elementary chips, and you will know how to test and compose these chips into larger designs. First, you will implement the 1-bit gates — Not, And, Or, Xor, Mux, and DMux — using only the Nand primitive. Second, you will create corresponding 16-bit versions that operate bitwise. Third, you will assemble multi-way selectors and demultiplexers such as Or8Way, Mux4Way16, Mux8Way16, DMux4Way, and DMux8Way. Fourth, you will run the Hardware Simulator test scripts, debug HDL errors, and verify that each chip passes its test cases. Each objective trains a specific skill: writing boolean logic and HDL, using modular design to manage complexity, and verifying correctness through systematic testing. For example, implementing Mux8Way16 teaches you how to reduce a multi-way selection into repeated use of simpler Mux16 components and reveals how many lower-level chips compose into a higher-level function. These objectives are practical checkpoints: completing them demonstrates competency in modular hardware design and verification.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Verification
screens.narratorSegment: Project 1 is as much about disciplined process as it is about logic. Your repeated practice will be: read the specification and truth table carefully; design the boolean expression or small circuit diagram; choose which built chips to reuse; write clear HDL with exact pin names; run the provided test script in the Hardware Simulator; and iterate until the tests pass. For example, when implementing Mux16 you will explicitly wire sixteen Mux components and name pins consistently so the simulator can connect them. The habit of composing and testing at each step is crucial because the hierarchy multiplies mistakes: a single miswired 1-bit gate can produce many failing 16-bit behaviors. To internalize this, keep a short log entry per chip noting the chosen decomposition and the debugging steps taken. This log becomes an audit trail and a study resource. The learning objectives therefore cover both building the chips and practicing verification discipline that scales to larger systems.

screens.title: Why start with Nand?
screens.narratorSegment: Starting from a single primitive is a deliberate pedagogical move. The Nand gate is universal: it can express Not, And, Or, and Xor functions when combined suitably. Project 1 uses only Nand as a primitive to force you to see how seemingly different gates are compositions of the same simple operation. The practical lesson is not that real chips are built this way in industry, but that the logical structure of computation reduces to a few basics. A concrete example: to build a Not gate you can connect both inputs of a Nand to the same signal. That transformation gives an inverter behavior with a single primitive. A common misconception is to assume starting with many gates is easier; in fact, starting with Nand makes you reason about construction and prevents you from treating gates as magical black boxes. When you later see multi-bit and multi-way chips, you'll recognize their repeated patterns and reuse smaller verified components. Reflect on this: if you can implement useful gates from Nand, you understand the logic behind them rather than memorizing behavior. Why start with Nand? means using only nand teaches construction and composition, revealing the underlying logic of every gate you build.. In practical terms, universality and the pedagogical choice behind project 1. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.6 › Why start with Nand?
Definition & claim
Nand is a universal primitive; building gates from it trains compositional thinking and verification habits.
Concrete transformation
Not(in) = Nand(in, in). This simple wiring turns a two-input Nand into an inverter by tying inputs together. That practice generalizes: show how other gates can be expressed by arranging Nand outputs and inputs.
Analogy
Think of Nand as a single brick shape. Complex walls follow from repeating a few brick patterns.
Misconception check
Industry uses many gate types for efficiency, but the logical universality of Nand remains a key teaching tool.
Visual example
Not from Nand
Tie both inputs of a Nand to the same signal; the Nand's output is then the inverted input. This small insight is the starting point for other constructions.
Why this matters
By forcing construction from one primitive you build mental models and avoid treating gates as prepackaged black boxes.

screens.title: Designing 1-bit gates: Not and And
screens.narratorSegment: Designing 1-bit gates begins with the specification and truth table. For Not and And, the steps are straightforward but instructive. Start by writing the truth table: for Not, map input values 0 and 1 to their inverted outputs; for And, list all (a,b) combinations. Next, express the desired function as a boolean form you can implement with Nand. For Not, tie both Nand inputs to the same signal. For And, recall that A and B equals Not(Nand(A,B)), so you can compute Nand(A,B) and then feed that result into a Nand again with both inputs tied to that intermediate output to invert it. When you write the HDL, choose concise internal wire names and ensure every pin is connected. A common mistake is incorrect pin names or missing wires; the simulator will flag these. After writing HDL, run the test script. If a case fails, inspect the simulator's internal view to see signal values through the composed chips. The concrete example is building And from Nand: implement Nand(a,b) as an internal output, then implement Not on that internal output to produce the final And output. That small composition pattern—compute then invert—is central and repeats often.

keyIdea.title: Compose small transforms
keyIdea.text: Implement And by computing Nand then inverting that result; implement Not by tying a Nand's inputs together.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.6 › Not and And
Step sequence
1
Write truth table
List input combinations and expected outputs for Not and And.
2
Derive boolean form
Not(x) = Nand(x,x). And(a,b) = Not(Nand(a,b)).
3
Write HDL and test
Name pins exactly, connect internal wires, run the test script, and debug failures.
Key Takeaway
Small compositions such as compute-then-invert are the reusable patterns you will apply repeatedly.
Concrete example
// And.hdl (conceptual)
CHIP And {
  IN a, b;
  OUT out;
  PARTS:
  Nand(a=a, b=b, out=n1);
  Nand(a=n1, b=n1, out=out);
}
Use the simulator to ensure that for all four input combinations the resulting out matches a and b conjunction. If a test fails, check internal wire n1 for expected values.

screens.title: Constructing Or and Xor from Nand
screens.narratorSegment: Or and Xor illustrate richer compositions built from Nand. For Or, use De Morgan's law: a OR b equals Not(Not(a) AND Not(b)). Implement this by first creating Not(a) and Not(b) with Nand tied-input patterns, then combine those with a Nand-based And followed by inversion as needed. This sequence shows how algebraic identities map to concrete HDL compositions. Xor is slightly more involved: it returns true when inputs differ. One standard construction uses combinations of Nand, Not, and And patterns to realize the exclusive-or logic. When you implement Xor in HDL using only Nand, break the function into small internal wires, name them clearly, and test intermediate signals when debugging. A common misconception is to try to write a single dense expression; instead, decompose into readable steps so the simulator can help you inspect each internal value. A concrete example: implement Not(a) and Not(b) as internals, compute aAndNotB and notAAndB as internals, then compute Or of those two to produce Xor. That readable decomposition both clarifies correctness and makes debugging straightforward. Constructing Or and Xor from Nand means use algebraic identities to map or and xor into small nand-based subcircuits with inspectable internal wires for debugging.. In practical terms, patterns for combining nand outputs into multi-gate logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.6 › Or and Xor
Or via De Morgan
a OR b = NOT( NOT(a) AND NOT(b) ). Build NOT(a) and NOT(b) from Nand, then compose an And and invert it.
Why decompose
Decomposing into named internal wires makes it easy to inspect each step in the Hardware Simulator and fix wiring or naming errors quickly.
Concrete tip
When debugging Xor, check intermediate terms like aAndNotB and notAAndB; the final Or of those internals should match expected exclusivity.
Example sketch
// Or.hdl (conceptual)
CHIP Or {
  IN a, b;
  OUT out;
  PARTS:
  Nand(a=a, b=a, out=na);
  Nand(a=b, b=b, out=nb);
  Nand(a=na, b=nb, out=n1);
  Nand(a=n1, b=n1, out=out);
}
Test for all input pairs. If a case fails, check na and nb values first to see if Not operations are correct.

screens.title: Mux vs DMux: routing signals
screens.narratorSegment: Multiplexers and demultiplexers route signals under selector control. A Mux outputs one of its inputs based on a selection bit: Mux chooses a when sel=0 and b when sel=1 for the 1-bit case. A DMux does the inverse: it takes a single input and sends it to one of two outputs depending on sel. Implementing Mux from Nand often uses the pattern of gating inputs with selectors and then combining results. For example, create notSel, then compute aAndNotSel and bAndSel, and finally OR those results to get the selected signal. DMux is similar: compute notSel and use it to gate the input into either the a or b output. When you scale to 16-bit Mux16, repeat the 1-bit Mux design across 16 lines and ensure consistent pin naming. A common mistake is misnaming selection pins or forgetting to gate every bit in the 16-bit case. A concrete example: when implementing Mux16, wire sixteen Mux chips in parallel, each receiving the same sel. If any single bit is miswired, the entire 16-bit word will be incorrect, so test both individual bit behavior and full-word behavior.

keyIdea.text: Mux and DMux are built by gating inputs with selection signals and composing results; parallelize the pattern for 16-bit versions.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.6 › Mux vs DMux
1-bit routing patterns
Mux: out = (a AND NOT(sel)) OR (b AND sel). DMux: route in to either a or b depending on sel, leaving the other output zero. Implement gating with Nand-based And and use Not where needed.
Common pitfall
For 16-bit variants, forgetting to apply the selection signal to every parallel gate causes word-level failures.
Concrete example
When building Mux16, instantiate sixteen Mux chips in parallel, each with the same sel input. Name wires like in[0]..in[15], out[0]..out[15], and use the exact pin names the simulator expects.
Key Takeaway
Routing logic is repetitive: design once for 1-bit, then parallelize carefully for multi-bit versions.

screens.title: Multi-bit chips: Not16, And16, Or16, Mux16
screens.narratorSegment: Multi-bit chips apply 1-bit logic in parallel across fixed-width registers. For Not16, And16, Or16, and Mux16 you replicate the corresponding 1-bit chip sixteen times and wire inputs and outputs as arrays of bits. The essential practices are consistent pin naming, using internal wires when helpful, and treating each bit independently so debugging remains localizable. For example, Not16 is simply sixteen Not components, each taking one bit and producing its inverted bit. Mux16 similarly uses sixteen Mux components, all sharing the same sel pin. A crucial point is exact pin names: HDL and the simulator are case-sensitive and expect precise identifiers. Another consideration is test coverage: for multi-bit chips you must test both per-bit behavior and full-word scenarios where patterns across bits matter. A common misconception is that multi-bit chips require new logic; instead, they are structured repetition. The hierarchy becomes clearer when you see that Mux16 is built from Mux, and later Mux4Way16 and Mux8Way16 are built from Mux16. Keep modules small and verified so that scaling to sixteen bits stays straightforward. Multi-bit chips: Not16, And16, Or16, Mux16 means multi-bit chips are parallel assemblies of 1-bit components; consistent naming and per-bit testing keep scaling manageable.. In practical terms, parallel composition and consistent pin naming. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scale by replication
keyIdea.text: Multi-bit chips are parallel assemblies of 1-bit components; consistent naming and per-bit testing keep scaling manageable.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.6 › Multi-bit chips
Design pattern
Replicate a 1-bit chip across 16 wires. Use consistent names like in[0]..in[15] or a[0]..a[15] as the project requires, and reuse the 1-bit HDL pattern inside a 16-bit wrapper.
Testing guidance
Test single-bit cases and full-word patterns (all zeros, all ones, alternating bits) to ensure per-bit wiring is correct.
Concrete example
Not16 is sixteen Not components. Mux16 is sixteen Mux components, each with the same selector. If one bit fails, inspect that bit's internal Mux instance and its input wiring immediately.
Key Takeaway
Scaling logic is mechanical once the 1-bit case is correct; verification of each parallel instance is what prevents subtle multi-bit bugs.

screens.title: Multi-way chips and the full project hierarchy
screens.narratorSegment: Project 1's hierarchy organizes chips by levels of composition. At the base sits Nand. The next level contains basic 1-bit gates like Not, And, Or, Xor, Mux, and DMux. Above that are 16-bit versions such as Not16, And16, Or16, and Mux16. The top layers include multi-way chips: Or8Way, Mux4Way16, Mux8Way16, DMux4Way, and DMux8Way. Each level reuses chips from the previous level in tested patterns. For instance, Mux8Way16 can be built by composing Mux4Way16 components and Mux16 components in a tree that reduces eight inputs down to one. The provided assessment example walks through Mux8Way16’s decomposition down to how many Mux16 and Mux components are required. Understanding this tree is important because it clarifies how many times a low-level bug will affect higher-level behavior. A common misconception is to attempt top-down design without verifying bottom-level primitives; the project enforces bottom-up verification. When you finish Project 1 you will have a small, well-tested library where each node in this hierarchy has a known behavior you can trust. Multi-way chips and the full project hierarchy means each higher-level chip is a node in a tree rooted at nand; verify leaves first so the whole tree is trustworthy.. In practical terms, from nand up to mux8way16 and or8way. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Design methodology: Understand → Design → Write → Test → Verify
screens.narratorSegment: Every chip you build should follow the same five-step methodology. First, understand the specification: read the chip description and commit to the truth table for all input combinations. Second, design the logic: choose a Boolean expression or small circuit diagram and decide which existing chips to reuse. Third, write the HDL carefully, with exact pin and internal wire names so the Hardware Simulator can parse connections. Fourth, test the chip by running the provided test script; inspect failing cases in the simulator's internal view. Fifth, verify correctness: ensure all test cases pass and the chip behaves as specified under representative inputs. A concrete example is building Mux4Way16: you first decide how to combine Mux16 and Mux chips, then write HDL that wires those components correctly, run the test script, and debug indexing errors or misnamed pins. A common mistake is skipping the design step and coding directly; that leads to brittle HDL and longer debugging. The power of this loop is that it scales: the same process works for a single Not gate and for an 8-way 16-bit multiplexer. Keep a short log for each chip documenting decisions and fixes; this habit turns one-off solutions into maintainable designs.

screens.title: Testing and the Hardware Simulator
screens.narratorSegment: The Hardware Simulator and the provided test scripts are your primary verification tools. A typical test script enumerates input cases and expected outputs; when a case fails, the simulator shows the internal wiring and the value of every wire in the composition. Use that internal view to find where a computed intermediate value diverges from expectation. For instance, if And16 fails for a particular bit pattern, inspect the internal Nand and Not instances for that bit to see whether the inversion step or the initial Nand produced the wrong signal. The simulator will also indicate connector errors like missing connections or wrong pin names. A helpful workflow is to test a chip first on simple partitions (single-bit or one pattern) before running the entire exhaustive script. Also, incrementally watch intermediate wires by giving them descriptive names in HDL; this makes the simulator output easier to read. A common misconception is to treat test failures as mysterious: in reality they point directly to incorrect internal wiring or naming. Use the simulator's internal view as a microscope that reveals where your composition departs from the specification.

screens.title: Common HDL mistakes and debugging strategies
screens.narratorSegment: There are a handful of recurring mistakes students make when writing HDL; recognizing them speeds debugging. First, wrong pin names are frequent because HDL is case-sensitive and expects exact identifiers. Always double-check that the external and internal pin names match the specification. Second, missing connections produce floating wires; if a wire is not driven by exactly one source, its value is undefined and tests will fail. The simulator will help you spot undefined values in the internal view. Third, circular connections create unintended feedback loops; Project 1 prohibits cycles because it is combinational logic. Confirm that the graph of connections is acyclic. A useful debugging strategy is to test each small component independently before integrating it into larger chips. For example, verify your Not and Nand compositions first; then use them inside And and Or. Keep descriptive internal wire names and a brief log of which test cases failed and what you changed to fix them. This log becomes invaluable if you later reuse the chip. Final tip: if tests repeatedly fail in higher-level chips, return to the lowest-level components and re-run their tests; the problem often originates there.

This chapter guides you through Project 1: creating a complete set of elementary logic gates using only the Nand gate and the chips you build along the way. You will produce 1-bit gates like Not, And, Or, Xor, Mux, and DMux, expand those designs into 16-bit versions, and assemble multi-way selectors and demultiplexers. The emphasis is on modular, hierarchical design: each chip is tested and verified before it becomes a building block for larger chips. Practically, this means translating truth tables into Boolean expressions, turning those into HDL, and using the Hardware Simulator with test scripts to confirm behavior. As you work, keep a concise log of design choices and debugging steps. This project is foundational: the chips you complete here function as the standard library for all later hardware in the course. By learning to reduce complexity to a single primitive and then composing verified components, you sharpen both engineering discipline and conceptual clarity. Reflect as you build: what does a computer become when you trace every operation back to one simple gate?

By the end of Project 1 you will have built a verified standard library of elementary chips, and you will know how to test and compose these chips into larger designs. First, you will implement the 1-bit gates — Not, And, Or, Xor, Mux, and DMux — using only the Nand primitive. Second, you will create corresponding 16-bit versions that operate bitwise. Third, you will assemble multi-way selectors and demultiplexers such as Or8Way, Mux4Way16, Mux8Way16, DMux4Way, and DMux8Way. Fourth, you will run the Hardware Simulator test scripts, debug HDL errors, and verify that each chip passes its test cases. Each objective trains a specific skill: writing boolean logic and HDL, using modular design to manage complexity, and verifying correctness through systematic testing. For example, implementing Mux8Way16 teaches you how to reduce a multi-way selection into repeated use of simpler Mux16 components and reveals how many lower-level chips compose into a higher-level function. These objectives are practical checkpoints: completing them demonstrates competency in modular hardware design and verification.

Project 1 is as much about disciplined process as it is about logic. Your repeated practice will be: read the specification and truth table carefully; design the boolean expression or small circuit diagram; choose which built chips to reuse; write clear HDL with exact pin names; run the provided test script in the Hardware Simulator; and iterate until the tests pass. For example, when implementing Mux16 you will explicitly wire sixteen Mux components and name pins consistently so the simulator can connect them. The habit of composing and testing at each step is crucial because the hierarchy multiplies mistakes: a single miswired 1-bit gate can produce many failing 16-bit behaviors. To internalize this, keep a short log entry per chip noting the chosen decomposition and the debugging steps taken. This log becomes an audit trail and a study resource. The learning objectives therefore cover both building the chips and practicing verification discipline that scales to larger systems.

Starting from a single primitive is a deliberate pedagogical move. The Nand gate is universal: it can express Not, And, Or, and Xor functions when combined suitably. Project 1 uses only Nand as a primitive to force you to see how seemingly different gates are compositions of the same simple operation. The practical lesson is not that real chips are built this way in industry, but that the logical structure of computation reduces to a few basics. A concrete example: to build a Not gate you can connect both inputs of a Nand to the same signal. That transformation gives an inverter behavior with a single primitive. A common misconception is to assume starting with many gates is easier; in fact, starting with Nand makes you reason about construction and prevents you from treating gates as magical black boxes. When you later see multi-bit and multi-way chips, you'll recognize their repeated patterns and reuse smaller verified components. Reflect on this: if you can implement useful gates from Nand, you understand the logic behind them rather than memorizing behavior. Why start with Nand? means using only nand teaches construction and composition, revealing the underlying logic of every gate you build.. In practical terms, universality and the pedagogical choice behind project 1. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Designing 1-bit gates begins with the specification and truth table. For Not and And, the steps are straightforward but instructive. Start by writing the truth table: for Not, map input values 0 and 1 to their inverted outputs; for And, list all (a,b) combinations. Next, express the desired function as a boolean form you can implement with Nand. For Not, tie both Nand inputs to the same signal. For And, recall that A and B equals Not(Nand(A,B)), so you can compute Nand(A,B) and then feed that result into a Nand again with both inputs tied to that intermediate output to invert it. When you write the HDL, choose concise internal wire names and ensure every pin is connected. A common mistake is incorrect pin names or missing wires; the simulator will flag these. After writing HDL, run the test script. If a case fails, inspect the simulator's internal view to see signal values through the composed chips. The concrete example is building And from Nand: implement Nand(a,b) as an internal output, then implement Not on that internal output to produce the final And output. That small composition pattern—compute then invert—is central and repeats often.

Or and Xor illustrate richer compositions built from Nand. For Or, use De Morgan's law: a OR b equals Not(Not(a) AND Not(b)). Implement this by first creating Not(a) and Not(b) with Nand tied-input patterns, then combine those with a Nand-based And followed by inversion as needed. This sequence shows how algebraic identities map to concrete HDL compositions. Xor is slightly more involved: it returns true when inputs differ. One standard construction uses combinations of Nand, Not, and And patterns to realize the exclusive-or logic. When you implement Xor in HDL using only Nand, break the function into small internal wires, name them clearly, and test intermediate signals when debugging. A common misconception is to try to write a single dense expression; instead, decompose into readable steps so the simulator can help you inspect each internal value. A concrete example: implement Not(a) and Not(b) as internals, compute aAndNotB and notAAndB as internals, then compute Or of those two to produce Xor. That readable decomposition both clarifies correctness and makes debugging straightforward. Constructing Or and Xor from Nand means use algebraic identities to map or and xor into small nand-based subcircuits with inspectable internal wires for debugging.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Multiplexers and demultiplexers route signals under selector control. A Mux outputs one of its inputs based on a selection bit: Mux chooses a when sel=0 and b when sel=1 for the 1-bit case. A DMux does the inverse: it takes a single input and sends it to one of two outputs depending on sel. Implementing Mux from Nand often uses the pattern of gating inputs with selectors and then combining results. For example, create notSel, then compute aAndNotSel and bAndSel, and finally OR those results to get the selected signal. DMux is similar: compute notSel and use it to gate the input into either the a or b output. When you scale to 16-bit Mux16, repeat the 1-bit Mux design across 16 lines and ensure consistent pin naming. A common mistake is misnaming selection pins or forgetting to gate every bit in the 16-bit case. A concrete example: when implementing Mux16, wire sixteen Mux chips in parallel, each receiving the same sel. If any single bit is miswired, the entire 16-bit word will be incorrect, so test both individual bit behavior and full-word behavior.

Multi-bit chips apply 1-bit logic in parallel across fixed-width registers. For Not16, And16, Or16, and Mux16 you replicate the corresponding 1-bit chip sixteen times and wire inputs and outputs as arrays of bits. The essential practices are consistent pin naming, using internal wires when helpful, and treating each bit independently so debugging remains localizable. A crucial point is exact pin names: HDL and the simulator are case-sensitive and expect precise identifiers. Another consideration is test coverage: for multi-bit chips you must test both per-bit behavior and full-word scenarios where patterns across bits matter. A common misconception is that multi-bit chips require new logic; instead, they are structured repetition. The hierarchy becomes clearer when you see that Mux16 is built from Mux, and later Mux4Way16 and Mux8Way16 are built from Mux16. Keep modules small and verified so that scaling to sixteen bits stays straightforward. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
